# Local cortex, untrained — 2026-11-17

*Generated by `npm run cortexeval`. Stage B1 of `design-plasticity-and-a-learning-cortex.md`. Test set: 2026-11-17 (held out by time), 120 examples where the act went well (60 of them hard moments: hostile near, night, or hungry) and 60 where it went badly. Menu of 26 acts. 3 sample(s) per example.*

| | Picks what worked | …in hard moments | Same kind of act | Steers clear of what went badly | Sure (all samples agree) | Right when sure | Right when unsure | Time per pick |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Random pick | 4% | 4% | — | 96% | — | — | — | — |
| Always "explore" | 16% | 3% | — | 85% | — | — | — | — |
| **gemma3:4b** | 18% | 15% | 18% | 77% | 93% | 18% | 11% | 0.4 s |
| **gemma3:12b** | 17% | 17% | 17% | 80% | 89% | 18% | 8% | 0.5 s |

**gemma3:4b** picked most: seekFood (87), flee (30), eat (26), returnInside (23), explore (13), approach (1). Invalid answers: 0.

**gemma3:12b** picked most: seekFood (93), eat (27), flee (27), idle (14), returnInside (11), move ahead (8). Invalid answers: 0.

- *Missed:* Daytime. Health 10/20, food 0/20. Where I stand: something over my head, 0 of 4 sides closed. I carry 2 kind(s) of block I could place. No hostile creature in sight. The edge of the world is 8.8 blocks away. — it did **idle** (went well); the model picked **seekFood**.

**How to read it.** "Picks what worked" is agreement with acts that went well, so it measures imitation of MindBot's own good moments, not whether the model would do *better*. That needs a live trial (B2). The useful signals here: is the model clearly above both baselines, especially in hard moments? Does being sure mean being right (if so, "unsure" is a good moment to hand off to Claude)? Is it fast enough to decide every few seconds?

## Laya (added later on 2026-11-17)

These are the same 180 held-out situations and the same 26-act menu (`agent/src/tools/laya_eval.py`, run in `agent/.venv-laya`). There are three contenders: Laya's small encoder (zero-shot), the vega engine (a frozen 0.8B Qwen 3.5 reader, zero-shot), and vega with a small head fitted on the **previous day's** 1,420 acts that went well. Laya serves a fitted head only if it beats the engine on held-out rows. The head was kept: cross-validated accuracy within that day was 53%, against the engine's 1% and chance at 4%.

| | Picks what worked | …in hard moments | Steers clear of what went badly | Time per pick |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Random pick | 4% | 4% | 96% | — |
| Always "explore" | 16% | 3% | 85% | — |
| gemma3:4b (above) | 18% | 15% | 77% | 0.4 s |
| gemma3:12b (above) | 17% | 17% | 80% | 0.5 s |
| Laya encoder, zero-shot | 11% | 15% | 98% | 0.02 s |
| Laya vega, zero-shot | 2% | 0% | 90% | 0.14 s |
| **Laya vega, fitted on one day** | **28%** | **27%** | 77% | 0.11 s |

The untrained engines mostly repeat one act: "move ahead" for the encoder, "place ahead" for vega. Their high "steers clear" scores are an artefact of that, not judgement. The fitted head picks varied acts: look for food (61), explore (55), flee (35), approach (12), stay put (8), walk back from the edge (5).

**Does its confidence mean anything?** Yes. Fitted Laya's calibrated confidence orders its picks well. Split into quarters by confidence, it was right 40%, 33%, 27% and 10% of the time, from most to least sure. Gemma's sample-agreement signal could not do that: Gemma was "sure" 90% of the time and right 18% of the time either way. This is what B2 needs to decide when to hand a decision to Claude. Laya's own strict route, which wants 95% precision, never triggers yet. Its sets of still-possible acts average 9 of 26: it is learning, not yet sure.

**Reading.** Learning is what makes the difference: untrained, every model is near or below the "always explore" baseline, and a few minutes of fitting on one day of MindBot's own life beats a 12-billion-parameter general model by about half again. The drop from 53% within the training day to 28% on the next day shows how much the days differ: a reset border, new plans, strict grading. More days and better labels should close some of that gap. Like every contender, it still repeats acts that went badly (77% steer-clear), because it learns only from what went well and the labels say little about what to avoid.

## A plain classifier (added later on 2026-11-17)

Is fitted Laya's gain Laya, or just fitting on MindBot's own day? Same fit day, same held-out test (`agent/src/tools/plain_eval.py`, `logs/training/plain-results.json`). Nothing new installed: the regression is PyTorch from Laya's environment.

| | Picks what worked | …in hard moments | Avoids what went badly | Time per pick | Right, by confidence quartile (most sure first) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Always the fit day's most common act (`explore`) | 16% | 3% | 85% | — | — |
| Lookup: most common act for the coarse situation (day/night, hostile near, hungry, hurt, sky open) | 23% | 20% | 78% | — | — |
| **Logistic regression** on words + the numbers (health, food, sides closed, nearest hostile, edge) | **33%** | 25% | 77% | 0.0005 s | 63%, 10%, 23%, 37% |
| Laya vega, fitted (for comparison) | 28% | 27% | 77% | 0.11 s | 40%, 33%, 27%, 10% |

Within its fit day (5-fold cross-validation) the regression scores 44% (Laya: 53%).

**Reading:** a plain classifier matches fitted Laya. With 120 good test rows, a 5-point difference is within noise, so call them even. It is about 200× faster and needs no 0.8B reader. Even a lookup table gets most of the way. The gain came from *fitting on MindBot's own life*, not from Laya. One thing Laya does better: its confidence falls steadily from most to least sure, while the regression's is only trustworthy in its most-sure quarter (63% right), then uneven. Both were fitted on one day only.
